Currently, ten states, including the state of California, allow some populations of undocumented immigrants to become professionally licensed in all or some occupations. For example, in California, undocumented immigrants can get any of 40 professional licenses available under state law so long as they meet all other eligibility requirements, and they can produce a federal individual Taxpayer Identification Number (ITIN) rather than a Social Security number (SSN). Other states’ laws about professional licensing for undocumented immigrants are generally less expansive than California’s law. For example, Florida and Illinois allow participants in the Deferred Action for Childhood Arrival (DACA) program to become licensed to practice law, although this may change with the upcoming demise of the DACA program. Wyoming also no longer requires that applicants for law licenses be U.S. citizens. New York allows teacher licenses and certifications for DACA recipients, and Nebraska allows DACA recipients to obtain all professional and commercial licenses. Nevada allows undocumented immigrants to obtain teaching licenses, South Dakota allows dentist licenses, and Utah allows occupational therapist licenses. Many states permit the professional licensing of undocumented immigrants in order to address occupational shortages, boost their economies, benefit from educational investment, and promote self-sufficiency for the immigrant population. This passage, as many of you already know, is called the Armor of God, and it contains six very specific items: the belt of truth, the breastplate of righteousness, sandals of the gospel of peace, the shield of faith, the helmet of salvation, and the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God.

Most of us, who follow Q, have taken this, and rightfully so, as a prayer request, but our prayers, if these forums are any indication at all, seem to be praying for things like protection (Trump), healing (COVID-19 patients), strength (military), and comfort (unemployed). Don’t stop, these are sweet, noble, sincere, and necessary prayers, but they are also quite passive in nature. I ask you; is someone suiting up with not just a few items but with the WHOLE (and the word “whole” is used twice in that passage for a reason) Armor of God expecting a passive encounter. No! The first five items are defensive: a belt, a breastplate, sandals, shield and a helmet. But the sixth item is a sword, an offensive weapon to be sure, and that weapon is the word of God or the Bible.

Weapons are not meant to heal or comfort, and only in a secondary sense are they meant to protect, a weapon is instead meant to inflict damage and to destroy. How can the Bible and our prayers be used offensively? Isn’t Christianity all about peace and love and meekness? If you have a sissified hippie-dippy notion of Christianity, you’re in the wrong religion. Christianity is for manly men and very strong women. Wimps need not apply! God used shepherds, a very rugged and lowly profession, as his prophets and kings. Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, Joseph, Moses, David, and Amos were all shepherds. Jesus used fisherman, another very rugged profession, as his disciples. Peter, Andrew, James and John, and possibly even others were all fisherman. The Bible has never described God’s chosen men as anything but virile.

So how does one pray offensively? Follow Nehemiah’s example! Nehemiah was a cupbearer for King Artaxerxes of Persia. He asked the king if he could return to Jerusalem and rebuild the wall; the king allowed this. Nehemiah and his men had to rebuild that wall with a sword in one hand because the enemy was nearby. Now pay attention to this. It was during this time that Nehemiah prayed this: “Hear us, our God, for we are despised. Turn their insults back on their own heads. Did you know the Bible contained words like that? Does that sound at all meek or peaceful? Building a wall while armed with a sword sounds rather manly and courageous to me. Nehemiah is asking God not only for the enemies’ complete destruction but for their humiliation as well. That does not sound like peace and love as we define it today. Jesus quoted from some of these imprecatory Psalms in the book of John so did the Apostle Paul in the Book of Romans, and even the Lord’s Prayer is imprecatory in nature! “Your kingdom come, your will be done, on earth as it is in. heaven,” asks God to set up an earthly kingdom immediately even if there are those who are not spiritually ready for eternity. That line, although it sounds so innocent, is actually asking for mass damnation. By the way, the Lord’s Prayer is self-imprecatory as well. “Forgive us our debts, as we also have forgiven our debtors.” This is asking God to judge us as harshly as we judge others. Did you know that that simple prayer was so dangerous?
